# STAT 110 (synthetic) — Midterm 1, 2025 (past paper)

**1.** Of 50 surveyed drivers, 30 own an electric car, and 12 of the electric
car owners charge at work. What percentage of electric car owners charge at
work?

**2.** Write the null and alternative hypotheses for testing whether the mean
commute time differs from 30 minutes, and state what a p-value of 0.03 means
at the 5% level.

**3.** A grouped summary computes the mean score for each of 4 sections of a
course with 120 students. How many rows does the result have?
materials.notes.md:
# STAT 110 (synthetic) — Lecture notes

## §1 Conditional probability

§1.1 P(A | B) is read "the probability of A among B". It answers: of the
cases in group B, what share are also in A?

§1.2 Compute it as (number of cases in both A and B) divided by (number of
cases in B). The denominator is the reference group B, not the whole sample.

§1.3 The order matters. P(A | B) and P(B | A) usually differ because they use
different reference groups. Before computing, decide which group the question
restricts you to; that group is the denominator.

§1.4 Assume every case is equally weighted and the reference group is not
empty.

## §2 Two-way tables

§2.1 A two-way table counts cases by two categorical variables at once, one in
the rows and one in the columns, with row totals and column totals.

§2.2 A row percentage divides a cell by its row total; a column percentage
divides a cell by its column total. Choosing row versus column percentages is
the same decision as choosing the reference group in §1.2.

§2.3 Row percentages in one row add to 100%; column percentages in one column
add to 100%. Percentages across a row of column percentages need not.

## §3 Grouped summaries

§3.1 A grouped summary splits the cases by a categorical variable and computes
one summary value (such as a mean or a count) per group.

§3.2 The result has one row per non-empty group, not one row per original case.

§3.3 Compare groups using the same summary; do not compare a group mean with a
group total.

# STAT 110 (synthetic) — Practice set A (T1 conditional probability)

Answer keys are in practice-key.md. Use the outline's reporting rule.

**Q1.** A class has 40 students. 25 of them commute. 10 of the commuters cycle
to campus. What percentage of commuters cycle?

**Q2.** A company has 60 employees. 24 of them work remotely. 6 of the remote
workers are trainees. What percentage of remote workers are trainees?

**Q3.** A club has 30 members. 12 of them are seniors. 4 of the seniors
volunteer at events. What percentage of seniors volunteer?

**Q4.** A store had 45 shoppers today. 20 of them ordered online. 9 of the
online shoppers returned an item. What percentage of online shoppers returned
an item?

responses.1:
I’ll check the materials folder and use your course’s notation and examples to explain conditional probability.

Conditional probability means updating a probability after learning that some event happened. The key idea is to treat that event as your new set of possible outcomes. I’m still waiting for the local file listing so I can connect this to your materials.

**Conditional probability asks: within a particular group, what percentage have the characteristic we care about?**

Your [notes, §1](materials/notes.md) write this as \(P(A\mid B)\), read “the probability of A **among B**.” The group after the bar, \(B\), is your **reference group**—it determines the denominator.

For equally weighted cases:

\[
P(A\mid B)=\frac{\text{number in both A and B}}{\text{number in B}}
\]

Consider Q1 in your practice set: a class has 40 students, 25 commute, and 10 of those commuters cycle. What percentage **of commuters** cycle?

We restrict attention to the 25 commuters. Of those, 10 cycle:

\[
\frac{10}{25}\times100\%=40.0\%
\]

So the answer is **40.0% of commuters cycle.** The full class size, 40, isn’t the denominator because the question restricts us to commuters.

Two things to remember:

- **Order matters:** “cycle among commuters” and “commute among cyclists” use different reference groups.
- **Name the group:** your midterm outline requires percentages rounded to **one decimal place**, with the reference group stated in words.

Try Q2: A company has 60 employees, 24 work remotely, and 6 remote workers are trainees. **What percentage of remote workers are trainees?** First identify your reference group, then calculate.
responses.2:
Your calculation gives **25.0% of all students who both commute and cycle**, but Q1 asks what percentage **of commuters** cycle.

“Of commuters” sets the reference group, so divide by the **25 commuters**:

\[
\frac{10}{25}\times100\%=40.0\%
\]

The answer is **40.0% of commuters cycle**.

Choose the denominator from the group the question asks about, rather than the first number mentioned.
responses.4: Correct—**33.3% of seniors volunteer at events**. You identified the reference group and used the 12 seniors as the denominator, independently.
responses.5:
Correct—**45.0% of online shoppers returned an item**. You chose the right denominator and stated the reference group.

Your independent answers to Q3 and Q4 show you understand conditional probability in these count problems. To check whether it carries over, try a different format next: a two-way table or a question that reverses \(P(A\mid B)\) and \(P(B\mid A)\).
responses.6:
A club has 50 members. Of its 20 seniors, 8 volunteer. Altogether, 16 members volunteer.

**What percentage of volunteers are seniors?**

State your reference group and report your answer as a percentage rounded to one decimal place.
responses.7:
Correct—**50.0% of volunteers are seniors**. You correctly used the 16 volunteers as the reference group.

Together with Q3 and Q4, this shows you can identify the denominator independently, even when the question reverses the groups. You’re ready to move on to conditional probability in two-way tables.
responses.8:
**Bayes’ rule lets you reverse the direction of a conditional probability:** from \(P(A\mid B)\) to \(P(B\mid A)\).

\[
P(B\mid A)=\frac{P(A\mid B)\,P(B)}{P(A)}
\]

The reference group changes when you reverse the condition, so you can’t simply swap the letters and keep the same answer.

Use our club example:

- **40.0% of members are seniors:** 20 out of 50.
- **40.0% of seniors volunteer:** 8 out of 20.
- **32.0% of members volunteer:** 16 out of 50.

Bayes’ rule gives:

\[
P(\text{senior}\mid\text{volunteer})
=\frac{P(\text{volunteer}\mid\text{senior})\,P(\text{senior})}
{P(\text{volunteer})}
=\frac{(8/20)(20/50)}{16/50}
=\frac{8}{16}.
\]

So **50.0% of volunteers are seniors**, exactly as you calculated earlier.

Here’s why it works: multiplying \(P(A\mid B)\) by \(P(B)\) gives the share of the whole population in **both groups**. Dividing by \(P(A)\) then changes the reference group to \(A\).

Your outline includes Bayes’ rule, but says the lecture notes are still to be posted; this is the standard rule.
responses.9:
Yes—but your **current outline explicitly excludes hypothesis testing** and says it moved to Midterm 2 this year. Last year’s midterm doesn’t reflect that change.

Hypothesis testing asks whether sample data provide enough evidence against a starting claim:

- **Null hypothesis (\(H_0\)):** the starting claim, often “no difference” or “no effect.”
- **Alternative hypothesis (\(H_a\)):** the competing claim you’re looking for evidence to support.
- **P-value:** assuming \(H_0\) is true, the probability of a result at least as extreme as the one observed.
- **Decision:** a sufficiently small p-value leads you to reject \(H_0\). Otherwise, you fail to reject it—which doesn’t prove it true.

For example, you might test whether a coin is fair by checking whether the observed number of heads would be unusually extreme for a fair coin.

For next week’s midterm, prioritize conditional probability, two-way tables, Bayes’ rule, and grouped summaries—the topics on your current outline.
